extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / citizens and delegates considering ratification (readers of The Federalist Papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative considerations for designing and judging a national executive (energy vs safety): which structural features — unity, duration, powers, accountability, etc. — make an Executive effective and republican. Drawn from Federalist No. 70 / No. 71 arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of energy in the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Energy in the Executive is essential to protection against foreign attacks, steady administration of the laws, protection of property, and security of liberty. The four listed components should be combined to produce an energetic executive without sacrificing republican safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity (single executive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is conducive to energy: decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity may be destroyed by vesting power in multiple magistrates of equal authority or by subjecting a nominal executive to controlling counsellors. A single executive is easier to watch, less able to combine broad influence, and less likely to produce factional dissension that weakens administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plurality / council (no executive council)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plurality in the Executive (multiple magistrates or an executive council) tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility; it introduces dissension, weakens authority, and may enervate administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plurality creates opportunities for mutual accusation, difficulty in assigning blame, expense (salaries/residence), and collusion. Councils can be a clog on good intentions, instruments of bad ones, and a cloak to faults; examples cited include appointment councils producing scandalous appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration (term length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration of office is an ingredient of executive energy; examples compare four years for a President to three years for a state governor, with remarks on how duration affects the establishment of dangerous influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer duration increases stability and reduces frequency of popular agitation, but must be balanced against republican safety (dependence and responsibility). The text argues four years for a national Chief Magistrate creates less risk of dangerous permanency than shorter terms at the state level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate provision for support
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate provision for the Executive's support is listed as an essential ingredient of energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not elaborated extensively in this chunk, the principle implies secure, sufficient compensation and material support so the executive can execute duties independently and effectively; the text also notes the public cost trade-offs when creating numerous officers or councils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent powers (powers adequate to duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive should possess competent powers — e.g., commander-in-chief of army and navy (and militia when in actual service), power to grant reprieves and pardons (except impeachment), recommend measures, convene/adjourn legislature on extraordinary occasions, take care that laws are faithfully executed, commission officers, make treaties with Senate consent, receive ambassadors, and appoint officers with Senate advice and consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent powers must be sufficient to enable energetic administration but structured to preserve republican checks (e.g., treaty-making with Senate concurrence; legislative authority over war and armies). The chunk compares these powers to those of the British king and state governors to illustrate scope and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety in the republican sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people, secondly, a due responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices should balance executive energy with mechanisms that ensure the executive remains dependent on the people (electoral mechanisms) and properly responsible (accountability and removal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Due dependence on the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Due dependence on the people is an ingredient of republican safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence is achieved through election and re-eligibility and by making the executive answerable to public opinion; this dependence constrains executive abuse while permitting energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due responsibility (personal responsibility / accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due responsibility requires that the magistrate be personally responsible for behavior in office, exposed to censure and punishment (impeachment, trial, ordinary prosecution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility has two kinds—censure and punishment—with censure being especially important in elective offices. A single executive makes detection and attribution of fault easier; plurality obscures responsibility and shifts blame among members. The President being impeachable, tryable, and punishable in ordinary law is contrasted with the inviolability of a hereditary monarch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment and ordinary prosecution as checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The President would be liable to be impeached, tried, and, upon conviction of treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors, removed from office; and would afterwards be liable to prosecution and punishment in the ordinary course of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal prosecutability is a critical republican safeguard absent for hereditary monarchs; it limits temptation and provides deterrence. The text uses this to contrast the proposed executive with the British sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto power structured with legislative override (qualified negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power to return a bill for reconsideration; the bill so returned is to become a law if, upon that reconsideration, it be approved by two thirds of both houses — a qualified negative different from the British absolute negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The qualified veto balances executive check on legislation with final legislative authority by supermajority override, contrasting with a monarch's absolute veto. The practical effect of non-use of absolute veto in Britain does not remove its existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on pardon power
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment; state governors (e.g., New York) may have different scopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting pardons (no pardon for impeachment cases) prevents the executive from shielding conspiracies from political accountability; the text contrasts presidential pardon scope with a governor's more extensive pardoning in practice and discusses political consequences of absolute pardoning authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment with legislative advice and consent; publicity of appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to nominate and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, appoint ambassadors, judges of the Supreme Court, and other officers; this mode entails publicity compared with private councils of appointment in some states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public appointment processes involving a larger body (Senate) are less easily influenced by private patronage than small, closeted councils. The chunk notes that small councils are easier to corrupt and that a divided Senate can block appointments, whereas some state governors with casting votes may confirm nominations unilaterally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making subject to legislative concurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be vested with power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties (provided two thirds of the senators present concur), rather than acting as sole representative as in the British model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involving the Senate in treaties limits unilateral executive foreign commitments. The chunk argues this federal arrangement gives the federal executive more power than state executives in treaty matters but less unilateral authority than the British sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander-in-chief authority and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This command is substantial but limited: the President's authority over militia is occasional (when called into service), and the power to declare war and raise/regulate fleets and armies is vested in the legislature. The comparison with the British monarch and some state governors clarifies differences in nominal vs substantive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception of ambassadors as a matter of dignity, not substantive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers; this is more a matter of dignity than of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structuring this power in the executive avoids convening the legislature for routine diplomatic formalities and has convenience/administrative value without significant policy-making consequences.
